Q1867: Capital of Taiwan, in the Taipei Basin in the north of the island; surrounded entirely by New Taipei City.
Seat of the Republic of China government since it retreated from the mainland in 1949.
Taipei 101 was the world's tallest building from 2004 to 2010; the National Palace Museum holds a huge collection of Chinese imperial art.
Q1070: The largest city in Gujarat, on the Sabarmati River; its twin city Gandhinagar is the state capital.
Founded in 1411 by Sultan Ahmad Shah; its old walled city is India's first UNESCO World Heritage City.
Gandhi's Sabarmati Ashram, starting point of the 1930 Salt March, is here.
Once called the 'Manchester of India' for its cotton mills; has the world's largest cricket stadium.
Q1297: The third-largest city in the USA, on Lake Michigan in Illinois.
Grew as the rail and shipping hub between the Great Lakes and the Mississippi; nicknamed the 'Windy City'.
Rebuilt after the Great Chicago Fire of 1871 and became the birthplace of the skyscraper.
Known for blues and jazz, deep-dish pizza, and the Willis (Sears) Tower.
Q1865: Capital of Malaysia, founded around 1857 as a tin-mining town where two rivers meet ('muddy confluence').
The Petronas Twin Towers were the tallest buildings in the world from 1998 to 2004.
The government moved most offices to the planned city of Putrajaya in 1999, but the parliament and king stay in KL.
A mix of Malay, Chinese and Indian cultures; the Batu Caves Hindu shrine is just north of the city.
Q10389: Capital of West Java, in a highland basin at about 700 m surrounded by volcanoes.
Hosted the 1955 Asian–African (Bandung) Conference, which led to the Non-Aligned Movement.
Developed by the Dutch as a cool resort city; nicknamed 'Paris of Java' and known for Art Deco buildings.
Home of the Bandung Institute of Technology (ITB), Indonesia's oldest technical university.
Q1858: Capital of Vietnam, on the Red River; the name means 'inside the rivers'.
Founded as Thăng Long ('ascending dragon') in 1010 as the capital of Đại Việt; the Imperial Citadel is a World Heritage Site.
Capital of French Indochina, then of North Vietnam; Ho Chi Minh's mausoleum is here.
Known for Hoàn Kiếm Lake, the Old Quarter's 36 streets, and phở.
Q42622: City in Jiangsu west of Shanghai, on the Grand Canal; called the 'Venice of the East' for its canals.
Its classical gardens, such as the Humble Administrator's Garden, are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
Founded in 514 BC; famous for silk, embroidery and Kunqu opera — 'Above is heaven, below are Suzhou and Hangzhou'.
Today a big high-tech manufacturing centre with the Suzhou Industrial Park.
Q4629: City in Gujarat on the Tapti River near the Arabian Sea; once the main port of the Mughal Empire.
About 90% of the world's diamonds are cut and polished here.
A major textile and synthetic fabric centre; the English East India Company set up its first Indian factory here in 1612.
One of the fastest-growing cities in the world.
Q1960: Tanzania's largest city and main port on the Indian Ocean; the name means 'abode of peace' in Arabic.
Founded by the Sultan of Zanzibar in the 1860s; capital of German East Africa and later Tanzania.
Lost its capital role to Dodoma, officially in 1996, but remains the economic centre.
The largest Swahili-speaking city and the largest city in East Africa.
Q1530: Capital of Iraq, on the Tigris River.
Founded in 762 by Caliph al-Mansur as the round city of the Abbasid Caliphate; home of the House of Wisdom.
In the Islamic Golden Age it was one of the largest cities in the world — the setting of many One Thousand and One Nights tales.
Q11720: Capital of Liaoning province and the largest city of Northeast China (Manchuria); its Manchu name was Mukden.
Early capital of the Manchu Qing dynasty; its Mukden Palace is a World Heritage Site.
The 1931 Mukden Incident here was Japan's pretext for invading Manchuria.
Q3692: Capital of Saudi Arabia, on the Najd plateau in the centre of the Arabian Peninsula.
Taken by Ibn Saud in 1902, the start of the conquest that created Saudi Arabia.
Grew from a walled mud-brick town to a city of millions since the 1950s, fuelled by oil wealth.
Diriyah, the original Saudi capital and a World Heritage Site, is on its edge; Riyadh will host Expo 2030.
Q170247: Capital of Shandong province, near the Yellow River.
Known as the 'City of Springs' for its 72 famous artesian springs, like Baotu Spring.
Mount Tai, one of China's five sacred mountains, lies just to the south.
Q8646: A special administrative region of China on the south coast, made of Hong Kong Island, Kowloon and the New Territories.
British colony from 1841 (after the First Opium War) until the handover to China in 1997; governed under 'one country, two systems'.
One of the world's leading financial centres, with the world's largest number of skyscrapers.
Victoria Harbour, the Peak and dim sum are icons; Cantonese and English are official.
Q1538: City in Maharashtra on the Deccan Plateau, about 150 km southeast of Mumbai; formerly spelled Poona.
Seat of the Peshwas, prime ministers of the Maratha Empire, in the 18th century; Shaniwar Wada was their palace.
Called the 'Oxford of the East' for its universities; a big IT and car-manufacturing hub.
Gandhi was interned at the Aga Khan Palace here in 1942–44.
Q87: Egypt's second city and main port, on the Mediterranean at the western edge of the Nile Delta.
Founded in 331 BC by Alexander the Great; capital of Ptolemaic Egypt and of Cleopatra.
Its ancient Lighthouse (Pharos) was one of the Seven Wonders, and its Great Library the biggest of antiquity.
The modern Bibliotheca Alexandrina revives the library.
Q170322: Port city in Shandong on the Yellow Sea; formerly spelled Tsingtao.
A German colony from 1898 to 1914 — hence its Bavarian-style buildings and the Tsingtao brewery (founded 1903).
Home of the appliance maker Haier.
Hosted the sailing events of the 2008 Beijing Olympics.
Q34647: South Africa's largest city and economic capital, in Gauteng province on the Witwatersrand ridge.
Founded in 1886 after gold was discovered; nicknamed 'Egoli', the City of Gold.
Soweto, centre of the anti-apartheid struggle, is part of the city; Nelson Mandela lived on Vilakazi Street.
Home of Africa's largest stock exchange and of the Constitutional Court.
Q42956: Capital of Heilongjiang province in China's far northeast, on the Songhua River.
Founded in 1898 by Russians building the Chinese Eastern Railway; Russian architecture like St. Sophia Cathedral remains.
Famous for its winter Ice and Snow Festival with huge illuminated ice buildings.
Has very cold winters, often below −20 °C.
Q2887: Capital of Chile, in the Central Valley between the Andes and the Coastal Range.
Founded in 1541 by Pedro de Valdivia; the Plaza de Armas was its original centre.
Home to over a third of Chile's population and nearly half its economy.
The snow-capped Andes are visible from the city; the Gran Torre Santiago is South America's tallest building.
Q16555: The largest city in Texas and the fourth-largest in the USA, near the Gulf of Mexico.
Named after Sam Houston, who won Texas independence from Mexico in 1836.
Centre of the US oil and gas industry; NASA's Johnson Space Center ('Houston, we have a problem') is here.
Home of the Texas Medical Center, the world's largest medical complex.
Q37995: Myanmar's largest city, formerly called Rangoon.
Capital until 2006, when the military government moved it to the new city of Naypyidaw.
The golden Shwedagon Pagoda is Myanmar's most sacred Buddhist site.
Has the largest number of British colonial-era buildings in Southeast Asia.
Q11462: Capital of East Java and Indonesia's second-largest city, a port on the Madura Strait.
Known as the 'City of Heroes' for the 1945 Battle of Surabaya against British troops, celebrated as Heroes' Day.
Main port of eastern Indonesia and a major naval base.
Its symbol is a shark (sura) fighting a crocodile (baya).
Q2807: Capital of Spain, in the centre of the Iberian Peninsula at about 660 m on the Manzanares River.
Became the permanent seat of the Spanish court in 1561 under Philip II.
The Prado, Reina Sofía and Thyssen museums form its 'Golden Triangle of Art'.
Home of football clubs Real Madrid and Atlético Madrid.
Q1963: Capital of Sudan, where the White Nile and the Blue Nile meet; forms one metro area with Omdurman and Khartoum North.
Founded in 1821 by the Egyptian ruler Muhammad Ali.
Captured by the Mahdists in 1885 after the siege in which British General Gordon was killed.
Heavily damaged in the civil war that began in 2023.
Q179295: The largest metropolitan area in Texas, built around Dallas and Fort Worth; locals call it the Metroplex.
Fort Worth grew as a cattle town ('where the West begins'); Dallas as a banking and trade centre.
President John F. Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas in 1963.
Home of the Dallas Cowboys and DFW Airport, one of the busiest in the world.
Q3624: Capital of Ethiopia, at about 2,355 m — the highest capital in Africa; the name means 'new flower'.
Founded in 1886 by Emperor Menelik II and his wife Taytu.
Headquarters of the African Union and the UN Economic Commission for Africa — often called the 'political capital of Africa'.
The National Museum holds 'Lucy', a 3.2-million-year-old hominin skeleton.
Q1515: The largest city and economic capital of Côte d'Ivoire, on lagoons along the Gulf of Guinea.
Capital until 1983, when Yamoussoukro became the official capital; most institutions and embassies stayed in Abidjan.
Became a major port after the Vridi Canal opened to the sea in 1951.
One of the largest French-speaking cities in the world; known for its Plateau business district.
Q172: Canada's largest city and capital of Ontario, on the shore of Lake Ontario.
Founded as York in 1793; renamed Toronto in 1834.
One of the most multicultural cities in the world: about half its people were born outside Canada.
The CN Tower was the world's tallest free-standing structure from 1975 to 2007.
Q59227: Historic city in eastern Guangdong, centre of the Teochew (Chaozhou) culture and dialect.
Ancestral home of millions of overseas Chinese in Southeast Asia, e.g. in Thailand and Singapore.
Known for Teochew cuisine, kung fu tea ceremony, and its ancient Guangji pontoon bridge.
Q3805: Capital of Jordan, originally built on seven hills.
Inhabited since the Neolithic: 'Ain Ghazal has some of the oldest human statues; later capital of the Ammonites (Rabbath Ammon).
Called Philadelphia in Greek and Roman times; a Roman theatre and the Citadel survive.
Grew from a small town after 1921 with waves of Palestinian, Iraqi and Syrian refugees.
Q8652: Coastal city in South Florida on Biscayne Bay; its metro area includes Fort Lauderdale and West Palm Beach.
About 70% of residents are Hispanic; Cuban exiles shaped neighbourhoods like Little Havana.
Known as the 'Capital of Latin America' for banking and trade, and for Miami Beach's Art Deco district.
Its port is the world's busiest cruise port.
Q42800: Capital of Minas Gerais state, built in the 1890s as Brazil's first planned modern city.
Replaced the colonial gold-mining town of Ouro Preto as the state capital.
Its Pampulha Complex by architect Oscar Niemeyer is a World Heritage Site.
Surrounded by mountains; known for its many bars ('botecos') and the Mineirão stadium.
Q74881: Port city at the southern tip of the Liaodong Peninsula in Liaoning.
Leased by Russia (as Dalny) and then held by Japan (as Dairen) from 1905 to 1945.
Its Lüshunkou district is the former Port Arthur, whose siege was the key battle of the Russo-Japanese War.
Known for its seaside parks, squares and summer Davos forum.
Q23556: Capital of Georgia (USA), in the foothills of the Appalachians.
Founded as a railroad terminus; burned by General Sherman's Union army in 1864.
Birthplace of Martin Luther King Jr. and a centre of the civil rights movement.
Headquarters of Coca-Cola, CNN and Delta Air Lines; its airport is the world's busiest by passengers.
Q334: A city-state on an island at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula, about 1° north of the equator.
Founded as a British trading post by Stamford Raffles in 1819.
Became independent in 1965 after being expelled from Malaysia; developed rapidly under Lee Kuan Yew.
One of the world's busiest ports and financial centres; official languages are English, Malay, Mandarin and Tamil.
Q30340: Capital of Henan province on the south bank of the Yellow River, in the 'cradle of Chinese civilization'.
Site of an early Shang-dynasty capital about 3,600 years ago.
A key railway junction where China's main north–south and east–west lines cross; nicknamed 'iPhone City' for Foxconn's huge factory.
The Shaolin Temple, birthplace of Shaolin kung fu, is nearby.
Q3870: Capital of Kenya; the name comes from the Maasai for 'place of cool waters'.
Founded in 1899 as a depot on the Uganda Railway.
The only capital with a national park inside its borders, where lions and giraffes roam with skyscrapers behind.
East Africa's business hub; hosts the UN Environment Programme headquarters.
Q28729: City on the Malabar Coast of Kerala, also called Calicut — the origin of the word 'calico'.
Vasco da Gama landed here in 1498, opening the sea route from Europe to India.
Medieval spice-trade port of the Zamorin kings, visited by Ibn Battuta and Zheng He.
UNESCO's first 'City of Literature' in India (2023).
Q174091: Capital of Hunan province, on the Xiang River.
Mao Zedong studied and began his political career here; Orange Isle has a giant statue of young Mao.
The Mawangdui tombs (2nd century BC) with their well-preserved mummy were found here.
Known for spicy Hunan food and stinky tofu.
Q179608: Capital of the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region in southern China, near Vietnam.
Called the 'Green City' for its subtropical greenery.
A centre of the Zhuang people, China's largest ethnic minority.
Hosts the annual China–ASEAN Expo, a gateway for trade with Southeast Asia.
Q182852: Capital of Yunnan province, at 1,900 m on the Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau.
Nicknamed the 'City of Eternal Spring' for its mild climate all year.
In WWII it was the end of the Burma Road and base of the American 'Flying Tigers' pilots.
The Stone Forest, a karst landscape, is nearby; Dian Lake lies south of the city.
Q1345: The largest city in Pennsylvania, on the Delaware River; nicknamed 'Philly'.
Founded in 1682 by the Quaker William Penn; the name means 'brotherly love' in Greek.
The Declaration of Independence (1776) and the US Constitution (1787) were signed at Independence Hall.
Home of the Liberty Bell and the cheesesteak.
Q3640: Capital of Turkey, in central Anatolia; Turkey's second-largest city.
Known in antiquity as Ancyra; capital of the Celtic Galatians and of a Roman province.
Atatürk led the War of Independence from here and made it the capital in 1923; his mausoleum, Anıtkabir, is a landmark.
The Angora goat, cat and rabbit are named after the city's old name.
Q1492: Capital of Catalonia, on Spain's Mediterranean coast; Spain's second city.
Antoni Gaudí's buildings, including the still unfinished Sagrada Família basilica, define its look.
Its Eixample district, with octagonal blocks, was planned by Ildefons Cerdà in the 1860s.
Hosted the 1992 Summer Olympics; home of FC Barcelona.
Q376749: Bangladesh's second city and main seaport, on the Karnaphuli River near the Bay of Bengal.
Its port, the busiest on the Bay of Bengal, handles most of Bangladesh's foreign trade.
An old trading port visited by Arab, Persian and Portuguese merchants.
Officially renamed Chattogram in 2018; gateway to the Chittagong Hill Tracts.
Q5838: Capital of Afghanistan, at about 1,800 m in a valley of the Hindu Kush on the Kabul River.
More than 3,500 years old; Babur, founder of the Mughal Empire, loved it and is buried in its Babur's Garden.
Badly damaged in the civil wars of the 1990s; under Taliban control again since 2021.
Q852238: Port city on the east bank of the Niger River in Anambra State, Nigeria.
Its Onitsha Main Market is one of the largest markets in West Africa.
A major Igbo trading centre, connected to Asaba by the Niger Bridge.
Known for 'Onitsha market literature', cheap pamphlet novels popular from the 1940s to 1960s.
Q656: Russia's second city, on the Neva River delta at the Baltic Sea; called Petrograd, then Leningrad (1924–1991).
Founded by Peter the Great in 1703 as Russia's 'window to Europe' and capital of the Russian Empire until 1918.
The October Revolution of 1917 began here; the city survived the 872-day Siege of Leningrad in WWII.
The Hermitage Museum in the Winter Palace is one of the largest museums in the world; known for its summer 'white nights'.
Q61: Capital of the United States, the District of Columbia, on the Potomac River between Maryland and Virginia.
Its site was chosen by George Washington; it became the capital in 1800, and the city plan was drawn by Pierre L'Enfant.
The White House, the Capitol and the Supreme Court are here.
The National Mall has the Lincoln Memorial, Washington Monument and the free Smithsonian museums.
Q3761: Capital of Ghana, on the Gulf of Guinea coast.
Grew around 17th-century European forts; capital of the British Gold Coast from 1877.
Ghana's independence in 1957, the first in sub-Saharan Africa, was declared here by Kwame Nkrumah.
Known for its markets, highlife music and the Independence Arch.
Q9022: Capital of Jalisco and Mexico's second-largest metro area; nicknamed the 'Pearl of the West'.
Founded in 1542 by the Spanish and named after Guadalajara in Spain.
Considered the birthplace of mariachi music and tequila (the town of Tequila is nearby).
A tech hub called the 'Mexican Silicon Valley'.
Q173985: Pakistan's third-largest city and main textile centre, in Punjab; formerly called Lyallpur.
Founded in the 1890s as a planned colonial city; its eight main bazaars radiate from a central Clock Tower, laid out like the Union Jack.
Renamed in 1977 in honour of King Faisal of Saudi Arabia.
Q188806: City at the northern tip of Kyushu, facing Honshu across the Kanmon Straits.
Formed in 1963 by merging five towns including the castle town of Kokura.
Birthplace of Japan's modern steel industry (Yawata Steel Works, 1901).
Kokura was the original target of the second atomic bomb in 1945; clouds diverted it to Nagasaki.
Q59100: Port city in eastern Guangdong, historically known as Swatow.
One of the treaty ports opened to Western trade in 1860.
One of China's first four Special Economic Zones (1980), because many overseas Chinese came from here.
Part of the Teochew (Chaoshan) cultural region, known for its cuisine and beef hot pot.
Q121157: Iran's second-largest city, in the northeast near Turkmenistan and Afghanistan.
The name means 'place of martyrdom': it grew around the shrine of Imam Reza, the eighth Shia imam.
The Imam Reza shrine is one of the largest mosques in the world and draws millions of pilgrims a year.
The poet Ferdowsi, author of the Shahnameh, is buried in nearby Tus.
Q58401: Capital of Hebei province, southwest of Beijing.
Grew from a village into a city only after railways met here in the early 20th century.
Nicknamed a 'city brought by trains'; became provincial capital in 1968.
A centre of China's pharmaceutical and textile industries.
Q3141: Capital of Victoria and Australia's second-largest city, on Port Phillip Bay.
Grew rich from the Victorian gold rush of the 1850s; was Australia's capital from 1901 to 1927.
Known for its laneway cafés, trams (the world's largest tram network) and sports: the Australian Open and Melbourne Cup.
Often ranked one of the world's most liveable cities.
Q612: The largest city of the United Arab Emirates, on the Persian Gulf coast.
Grew from a pearling village into a trade hub; oil, then tourism, trade and finance made it boom.
The Burj Khalifa (828 m) is the tallest building in the world; the Palm Jumeirah is an artificial island.
About 9 in 10 residents are foreign nationals.
Q81033: Capital of Nuevo León and Mexico's main industrial city, at the foot of the Sierra Madre Oriental.
Founded in 1596; the saddle-shaped Cerro de la Silla mountain is its symbol.
Headquarters of big companies like Cemex and FEMSA; close ties with Texas.
Known for cabrito (roast goat) and the Fundidora steelworks turned into a park.
